prompt: In a typical modern x86 desktop CPU, which cache level is shared across all cores on the same chip?
choices: L1
L2
L3
None — all cache levels are private per core

prompt: Using typical latencies (L1 ~1 ns, DRAM ~90 ns), roughly how much slower is a DRAM access than an L1 hit?
choices: About 2x
About 10x
About 30x
About 80-100x

prompt: What physically stores a single bit in a DRAM cell, as opposed to an SRAM cell?
choices: A cross-coupled pair of inverters (6 transistors)
A single capacitor plus one access transistor
A flip-flop built from NAND gates
A resistive memory element (memristor)

prompt: Why does DRAM need periodic refresh but SRAM does not?
choices: DRAM runs at a lower voltage, which corrupts data over time
DRAM's capacitor-based bit cells leak charge and must be rewritten every ~64 ms or the stored value decays
SRAM has built-in error correction that DRAM lacks
DRAM cells physically wear out after each read

prompt: A cache-latency benchmark uses pointer chasing (each load's address depends on the value just loaded) instead of a simple sequential array scan. Why?
choices: Pointer chasing is easier to code
Sequential access lets the hardware prefetcher fetch ahead and hide real miss latency, so measured times would reflect bandwidth rather than true per-access latency
Pointer chasing uses less memory
Sequential access always causes TLB misses

prompt: In the pointer-chase benchmark's staircase output, the average ns/access jumps sharply once the working set outgrows the L2 size. What does that jump correspond to?
choices: The working set now mostly resides in L3 instead of L2
The CPU has switched from paging to segmentation
The benchmark has hit a compiler optimization boundary
The jump is an artifact with no relation to cache size

prompt: A 2D array `float m[4096][4096]` is stored in row-major order in C. Which traversal has better spatial locality?
choices: Column (j) in the outer loop, row (i) in the inner loop
Row (i) in the outer loop, column (j) in the inner loop, so consecutive inner-loop accesses are adjacent in memory
Locality is identical either way since it's the same data
Neither — C stores 2D arrays non-contiguously

prompt: DDR4-3200 has a CAS latency (CL) of 16 clock cycles, measured at the DRAM's 1600 MHz base clock. What is CL in nanoseconds?
choices: 5 ns
10 ns
16 ns
20 ns
